rv.q: This mix of sumptuousness and precision is typical of Marianne Elliott's sweeping staging of scandalous French classic Les Liaisons Dangereuses
It is a leisurely evening but full of savour.
It's a great cast for this fascinating, if chilling, play
But it’s a curious piece: very easy to admire; harder to love.
A moral story at its core, the story builds to the mutual destruction of both its central villains, by which time this stylish production has finally found its dark, menacing heart.
As a drama, it emerges as elegant and divertingly nasty; it needs to matter more.
Its newfound elan is thanks to a sizzling cast led by the sublime Janet McTeer and a bolder take on the piece from Rourke.
Marianne Elliott’s production isn’t short of spectacle.
What can I say: it’s a really good production with two sensational leads, of a play that has long stopped being a sexy novelty and now kind of sits as a guilty pleasure.
But the sinister music as he coerces her into bed is part of a production reluctant to let us come to our own conclusions.
What is perhaps surprising is that, just by
Elliott’s refreshing vision only becomes more gripping as the scheme unfolds.
Beneath the play’s Wildean bon mots, champagne and glamour, there lurks a dark heart and all-consuming destructive devastation.
There is real danger, real excitement and delicious malicious jeopardy in spades.
Manville is magnificent and really gets her teeth into the woman who is both cruel and highly manipulative.
Manville and Turner are simply superb, their performances deep and thoughtful.
It is awash with dance, the scripted scenes interrupted by these self-consciously louche and postering performers.
Manville’s Marquise is regal, in both dress and demeanour, commanding the stage as she uses her charms to commandeer the play’s events
Whatever your interpretation, this much is sure: you are in for a wickedly sumptuous show.
Les Liaisons Dangereuses is a wonderfully cast romp through a razor-sharp period piece which doesn’t quite convince of its relevance to today.
Manville and Turner are phenomenal.
Dark, seductive and sharply observed, this is a revival that both entertains and unsettles.

cn.t: Manville and Turner lead a sumptuous, stylish revival that mostly captivates with its cruel seductions, though some critics question its modern relevance and find the central chemistry surprisingly tepid.
